2026 SEMA Show • Ringbrothers Mesmerizes the SEMA Show Once Again, This Time With Billie, the 650-HP Pontiac GTO
One-of-None 1970 Hemi Challenger Rocks Coolest Dealer-Installed Accessory, Two Owners in 56 Years
91 photos
Photo: YouTube/DezzysSpeedShop
Back in 1969, Detroit engineers apparently substituted their morning coffee with high-octane leaded fumes, looked at a brick-shaped coupe, hammered a towering stabilizer onto the trunk, and declared war on physics. That glorious corporate fever dream birthed the winged aero warriors that every collector worships today, the fabulous Charger Daytona (and its subsequent sibling, the 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird). Yet someone in California wanted a 1970 Dodge Challenger R/T 426 Hemi with a genuine Charger Daytona wing right from the dealership showroom floor. And he got it.
Before purists faint into their restoration manuals, let us state the obvious: Dodge never offered a towering wing on the Challenger, making this machine a glorious one-of-zero anomaly. In fact, no American pony car ever received a skyscraper stabilizer from the factory, as Detroit reserved such aerodynamic lunacy strictly for intermediate B-body racers from Ma Mopar. Yet when Troy Bergeron of the Mopars5150 YouTube channel examined this coupe, its wild past proved undeniable.
Understanding how a towering aluminum clothesline ended up on an E-body requires revisiting 1969, when Dodge unleashed the Charger Daytona for just one model year to conquer NASCAR ovals. Realizing that standard Chargers possessed the aerodynamic efficiency of a flying sack of bricks near 200 mph (322 kph), Chrysler summoned its aerospace division brainiacs.
Rocket scientists grafted on a pointy nose cone (hey, a missile needs to be pointy to look mean, right?) and a 23-inch (584-millimeter) rear wing that reached clean, undisturbed air while also clearing the trunk lid. Though the luggage space acccess was never considered, the wing's height happily checked that issue off the list of problems the Charger Daytona could've had.
Homologation rules only forced Dodge to build 503 examples of the 1969 Charger Daytona for showroom duty, comprising 433 cars equipped with the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Magnum V8 and a mere 70 packing the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8. Plymouth followed suit for the 1970 season with 1,935 Road Runner Superbirds, including 135 Hemi cars, before NASCAR banned the aero warriors into oblivion. Meanwhile, Dodge finally remembered that compact pony cars existed.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Arriving fashionably dead last to the pony car brawl on September 25, 1969, the 1970 Dodge Challenger stretched its E-body wheelbase 2 inches (51 millimeters) beyond the Plymouth Barracuda while sharing nada exterior body panels with its sibling. Across five model years from 1970 through 1974, U.S. production reached 165,437 units, with 76,935 for 1970 alone. Then the whole fashion went really South really fast: 26,299 for 1971, 22,919 for 1972, 27,930 for 1973, and 11,354 before ending in April 1974.
To compensate for showing up late, Dodge stuffed everything from docile 225-cubic-inch (3.7-liter) Slant Six-cylinder engines to the earth-shattering 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8 rated at 425 horsepower (431 PS) under the Challenger hood. Out of 18,512 Challenger R/T models built for 1970, only 356 received the Hemi, including 287 hardtops, 60 Special Edition coupes, and nine convertibles, with 154 featuring automatic transmissions, before Hemi production plunged to 71 cars for 1971.
This particular R-code heavyweight rolled off the Hamtramck, Michigan assembly line in November 1969 as 1 of only 150 non-SE 1970 Hemi Challenger R/T hardtops fitted with the 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic. Verified by its original broadcast sheet, fender tag, and core support stamping JS23R0B193316, the coupe wore Go Mango paint alongside the 426 Hemi, a Performance Axle Package, and California emissions equipment.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 When the original buyer bought the beast in July 1970 through a military credit union, dealership mechanics indulged his glorious lack of restraint by bolting a genuine 1969 Charger Daytona wing directly onto the rear quarters. Using four bolts per upright and zero internal trunk braces, that installation risked buckling the sheet metal at high speed. Vintage Polaroids found inside the trunk confirm it wore that wing from day 1.
Even the California Department of Motor Vehicles joined the comedy routine by issuing sequential 1970 blue license plates reading 426 BPW, accidentally matching the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) elephant under the hood. Naturally, owning a winged Hemi Challenger with a "426" plate demanded immediate high-speed validation, including a fabled dealership-backed run on the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, where the original factory engine promptly celebrated its freedom by grenading itself in 1970.
Because the mechanical fireworks happened while the car was still fresh off the lot, Chrysler graciously supplied a hydraulic-lifter warranty replacement 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi block carrying a riveted teal tag and factory broach marks stamped only with T and A. Although a dark blue oil pan sparked rumors of a marine engine, Bergeron proved the block was unpainted factory iron topped by its original $3,500-apiece dual 4-barrel Carter AFB carburetors.
Photo: YouTube/DezzysSpeedShop As if the towering Dodge Scat Pack Club wing and "426 Hemi 660" hood emblems were too subtle, someone slapped a 200 mph (322 kph) decal over the 160 mph (257 kph) Rallye speedometer, which reads 3,942 miles (6,344 kilometers) despite an estimated 30,000 miles (48,280 kilometers) traveled. Inside, the working key buzzer, Rim Blow wheel, and 1990s black-and-orange upholstery complement an older pearl-tinted orange respray, window louvers, and California exhaust turndowns.
The original owner treasured his winged anomaly for 49 years until chemotherapy forced a sale to a close friend in 2019, complete with unmounted tires dated August 2005 stacked inside his kitchen. Over the next several years, the second caretaker drove it barely 10 miles (16 kilometers) due to mushy drum brakes, while a $1,200 recore needed for its 956 radiator, $50 hourly shop rates, and steep pricing deterred Bergeron.
After having just 2 owners across 56 years, the rust-free survivor retaining its factory Hemi torque boxes and collapsible spare tire suddenly became the hottest ticket on the market. Purchased on August 14, 2026, and flipped again on August 20, 2026, the coupe doubled its ownership roll call in 5.6 days before heading toward Ohio, standing forever as hilarious proof that in 1970, one could order their car exactly as they wanted it.
